A claim circulating on social media alleges that autopsies conducted in Russia revealed that Covid-19 is not caused by a virus, but rather by a bacterium. According to the post, Russian authorities supposedly discovered this after performing autopsies on Covid-19 victims, and the finding contradicts the global scientific consensus that Covid-19 is a viral disease. This article examines the accuracy of this claim by reviewing established scientific knowledge, the process of Covid-19 identification, and the plausibility of such autopsy results.

The assertion that Covid-19 is a bacterium fundamentally misrepresents the nature of the disease. Covid-19 is the illness caused by the novel coronavirus, officially named SARS-CoV-2. This virus was first identified in late 2019 in Wuhan, China, where scientists isolated it from patients with pneumonia of unknown cause. Detailed genetic sequencing revealed that the pathogen was a new member of the coronavirus family, which are well-known RNA viruses responsible for respiratory illnesses such as SARS and MERS.

The identification of SARS-CoV-2 as a virus was not limited to China. Scientists worldwide, including in Russia, have studied the virus using advanced molecular biology techniques. These methods include polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests, which specifically detect viral RNA, as well as electron microscopy and viral culture. The entire genomic sequence of the virus has been publicly available since early 2020, allowing laboratories across the globe to confirm its identity and characteristics independently.

Autopsies have played an important role in understanding the effects of Covid-19 on the human body. Post-mortem analyses have revealed how the virus damages lung tissue and sometimes leads to complications such as blood clots. In rare cases, secondary bacterial infections have been observed in severely ill patients, but these are understood to be complications rather than the primary cause of the disease.

No credible reports from Russian health authorities or scientific institutions support the claim that autopsies in Russia found Covid-19 to be bacterial in nature. Russian scientists and physicians have consistently described Covid-19 as a viral disease, and Russia’s approach to testing, treatment, and vaccine development has been based on the understanding that SARS-CoV-2 is a coronavirus. Furthermore, the World Health Organization and health agencies worldwide—including those in Russia—have categorized Covid-19 as a viral pandemic.

It is possible that the confusion stems from misunderstandings about the role of secondary bacterial infections in Covid-19 patients. In some severe cases, individuals develop bacterial pneumonia as a complication, but this does not change the fact that the underlying cause is a viral infection. Antibiotics—which target bacteria—are not effective against viruses and are not prescribed for the treatment of Covid-19 itself, except in cases of confirmed bacterial co-infection.

In summary, the claim that Russian autopsies revealed Covid-19 to be a bacterium is not supported by scientific evidence or official statements. Covid-19 is unequivocally caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, as confirmed by extensive global research, including in Russia. Misinformation of this sort can contribute to confusion and undermine public health efforts. It is important to rely on verified scientific information and guidance from reputable health organizations.

A social media post has recently circulated, claiming that a document proves "Corona" already existed in 1985 in the German Democratic Republic (GDR, or East Germany). The post suggests that the current coronavirus pandemic is not as novel as widely reported, hinting at prior knowledge or even a cover-up. This fact-checking article investigates the veracity of the claim by examining the context, terminology, and available evidence.

The claim builds on the discovery of an old document—often a textbook or veterinary manual—from the GDR era. Images of such documents, sometimes accompanied by highlighted passages, have been shared online. These passages mention “Corona” or “coronavirus” in relation to diseases in animals. Some interpretations on social media leap to the conclusion that this references the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2, and therefore casts doubt on the novelty of the current coronavirus.

To understand this claim, it is important to distinguish between the coronavirus family and the specific virus causing COVID-19. Coronaviruses are a large family of viruses, some of which cause illness in humans and animals. They were first identified in the 1960s. Prior to the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, several coronaviruses were already known to infect humans, causing mild illnesses like the common cold. In animals, coronaviruses have long been recognized as causes of diseases such as infectious bronchitis in poultry, feline infectious peritonitis in cats, and transmissible gastroenteritis in pigs.

In the context of the GDR document, references to “Corona” or “coronavirus” are not unusual or secretive. Veterinary and medical science in the 1980s already recognized coronaviruses as pathogens in animals. The use of the term “Corona” in a 1985 document from East Germany is entirely consistent with the scientific understanding of the time. It does not indicate the presence of the novel coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, in humans, nor does it suggest prior knowledge of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The confusion often arises from the use of the word “Corona” as shorthand for the virus responsible for the pandemic. In scientific terminology, “coronavirus” refers to the broader family, not just the specific virus behind COVID-19. The current pandemic is caused by a novel member of this family, identified in late 2019. No credible evidence suggests that SARS-CoV-2, or anything genetically identical to it, was known or circulating in humans in 1985.

The post’s core claim, that a document “proves” Corona existed in the GDR in 1985, is misleading. While it is true that coronaviruses were documented and discussed in scientific literature decades ago, this does not undermine the novel nature of the virus causing COVID-19. The documents in question simply reflect the established scientific knowledge of their time.

In conclusion, the referenced GDR document does not prove that the current coronavirus pandemic was known or anticipated in 1985. It only confirms that the coronavirus family, particularly those affecting animals, was already recognized by scientists. The claim conflates general scientific terminology with the specifics of the ongoing pandemic, resulting in a misleading narrative.

A claim circulating on social media alleges that German Health Minister Karl Lauterbach stated, “death cases must be accepted for a successful vaccination campaign,” or that “the possibility of people dying as a consequence of vaccination must be accepted to achieve a successful vaccination campaign.” This assertion has raised alarm, prompting questions about the ethics and safety of vaccination campaigns, as well as the veracity of the statement itself. In this fact-checking analysis, we examine the origins of the claim, provide context about Karl Lauterbach’s public statements, and assess the accuracy of the alleged quote.

**Background and Context**

Karl Lauterbach, a physician and professor of health economics, has served as Germany’s Federal Minister of Health since December 2021. Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, Lauterbach has been a visible public figure, advocating for vaccination as a key tool in combating the virus and reducing severe illness and death. His public remarks have consistently emphasized the importance of vaccine safety and monitoring, acknowledging that, like all medical interventions, vaccines can have side effects, but that the benefits far outweigh the risks.

**Analysis of the Claim**

To evaluate the claim, it is necessary to determine whether Lauterbach has ever made a statement explicitly or implicitly suggesting that deaths caused by vaccines are an acceptable price for a successful vaccination campaign.

A review of public records, interviews, press conferences, and parliamentary speeches reveals no instance where Karl Lauterbach has made such a statement. In fact, he has repeatedly stressed the rigorous safety standards applied to vaccines in Germany and the European Union, underscoring the responsibility of authorities to monitor and respond to any adverse effects. He has acknowledged, in line with scientific consensus, that very rare and serious side effects, including deaths, can occur with any medical treatment, including vaccines. However, in these discussions, Lauterbach has not framed such events as something “to be accepted” in the pursuit of vaccination goals, but rather as risks to be minimized through strict oversight, transparency, and compensation mechanisms for those affected.

**Origin and Spread of the Claim**

The claim appears to have originated from a distortion or misinterpretation of general statements about risk-benefit analysis in public health. In vaccine policy, it is standard to communicate that, while severe adverse events are extremely rare, the benefits of preventing widespread disease and death outweigh the minimal risks associated with vaccination. Some opponents of vaccination have taken such explanations out of context, reframing them as callous acceptance of death, rather than as a sober assessment of relative risk.

No evidence can be found in any credible source—news reports, official transcripts, or video recordings—where Lauterbach is on record making the statements attributed to him in the social media post.

**Conclusion**

The claim that Karl Lauterbach stated “death cases must be accepted for a successful vaccination campaign,” or that deaths due to vaccination must be accepted to achieve vaccination goals, is not supported by evidence. Lauterbach has acknowledged, in line with public health practice, the necessity of weighing risks and benefits, but there is no record of him making the alleged statement or expressing such a sentiment. The claim appears to be a misrepresentation of standard public health communication.

Toto tvrdenie vyvolalo obavy, čo viedlo k otázkam ohľadom etiky a bezpečnosti kampaní očkovania, ako aj pravdivosti samotného tvrdenia. V tejto analýze pravdy si vysvetlíme pôvod tohto tvrdenia, poskytneme kontext o verejných vyjadreniach Karla Lauterbcha a overíme pravdivosť uvedeného citácie.

**Pozadie a kontext**

Karl Lauterbach, lekár a profesor zdravotnej ekonomiky, bol od decembra 2021 nemeckým ministerom zdravotníctva. Počas pandémie koronavírusu bol Lauterbach viditeľnou osobou v verejnom živote, ktorý sa zaviazal k očkovaniu ako kľúčovému nástroju boja proti vírusu a zníženiu vážnych prípadov ochorenia a smrti. Jeho verejné vyjadrenia vždy zdôrazňovali dôležitosť bezpečnosti očkovania a monitorovania, uznávajúc, že, ako každá lekárska liečba, očkovania môžu mať vedľajšie účinky, ale zisk prekračuje riziká.

**Analýza tvrdenia**

Na vyhodnotenie tohto tvrdenia je potrebné zistiť, či Karl Lauterbach niekedy explicitne alebo implicitne vyjadril názor, že smrty spôsobené očkováním sú prijateľným cienou pre úspešnú kampaň očkovania.

Prehľad verejných záznamov, rozhovorov, tlačových konferencií a prednášok v parlamente nedáva žiadnu príležitosť, kedy by Karl Lauterbach vyslovil takéto tvrdenie. Naopak, opakovaným spôsobom zdôraznil náročné štandardy bezpečnosti aplikované na vakcíny v Nemecku a v EÚ, zdôrazňujúc zodpovednosť orgánov na monitorovanie a reakciu na akékoľvek škodlivé účinky. Uznal v súlade s vedeckým konsenzom, že veľmi zriedkavé a vážne vedľajšie účinky, vrátane smrti, môžu vyskytovať sa pri akomkoľvek lekárskom liečení vrátane vakcíny. V týchto diskusia však Lauterbach neformuloval takéto udalosti ako niečo, čo by „muselo byť prijaté“ na dosiahnutie cieľov očkovania, ale radšej ako riziká, ktoré sa musia minimalizovať prostredníctvom náročného dozoru, transparentnosti a kompenzačných mechanizmov pre postihnutých.

**Pôvod a šírenie tvrdenia**

Tvrdenie zdá sa vzniknúť z zavádzania alebo nepresného pochopenia všeobecných vyjadrení o analýze rizik a výhod v verejnom zdravotníctve. V vakcínnych politikách je zvyčajné komunikovať, že aj výrazné nežiaduce udalosti sú veľmi zriedkavé, ale zisk z zabránenia šíreniu šíreniu ochorenia a smrti prekračuje minimálne riziká spojené s očkovaním. Niektorí očkovacie opozičníci si však vytiahli takéto vysvetlenia z kontextu a preformulovali ich ako chladnokrvnú prijatie smrti, namiesto ako reálne hodnotenie relatívneho rizika.

The claim that vaccination certificates were planned 20 months before the outbreak of the Coronavirus has circulated widely on social media, raising questions about the timing and motivations behind the introduction of such policies. This article examines the origin of this claim, provides context around vaccination certification, and evaluates its accuracy based on available information.

The core assertion suggests that authorities or organizations had already planned for the introduction of vaccination certificates nearly two years before the first public reports of COVID-19 emerged in late 2019. This, according to the claim, implies a degree of foreknowledge or premeditation regarding the pandemic or the measures that would become central to the global response.

To analyze this claim, it is essential to understand the history and evolution of vaccination certificates. The concept of certifying immunization status is not new. For decades, the World Health Organization (WHO) has required proof of vaccination against certain diseases for international travelers, most notably with the “International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis” (often called the Yellow Card) for diseases such as yellow fever. These certificates have been a staple of international travel regulations and public health for many years, well before the emergence of COVID-19.

The specific reference to a timeline—20 months before the coronavirus outbreak—likely refers to discussions or documents from international health bodies or organizations exploring digital health credentials and improving immunization records. In 2018, for example, there were initiatives and pilot projects focused on digital vaccination records, driven by advances in technology and the need to streamline health documentation. These projects aimed to address challenges in tracking vaccinations for diseases like measles, polio, and influenza, particularly in global travel and public health efforts.

However, there is no evidence that these initiatives were connected to or motivated by foreknowledge of the COVID-19 pandemic. Instead, they emerged from longstanding public health needs and technological advancements. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the implementation and expansion of digital vaccination certificates, but the groundwork for such systems existed due to evolving international travel requirements, improvements in digital health infrastructure, and efforts to combat existing infectious diseases.

Furthermore, the nature of the COVID-19 vaccination certificates introduced in 2020 and 2021 was distinct from previous systems. They were designed specifically to address the unique challenges posed by the pandemic, such as mass immunization campaigns, new vaccine technologies, and the need for rapid, secure verification of immunization status for access to public spaces and international travel.

In summary, while there were discussions and pilot projects regarding vaccination certificates prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, these were not specifically planned in anticipation of a coronavirus outbreak. The claim that vaccination certificates were intentionally planned 20 months ahead of COVID-19 misconstrues the historical context of immunization documentation and the evolution of digital health technologies. The expansion of vaccination certificates during the pandemic was a response to emergent needs, not evidence of prior knowledge or planning for COVID-19.

In recent days, a claim has circulated on social media alleging that the Covid-19 vaccination of German actress Uschi Glas was staged for a government vaccination campaign video. The post suggests that the vaccination event was not authentic, implying that the campaign misrepresented her receiving the vaccine. To evaluate the veracity of this claim, it is crucial to consider the context of the campaign, the events surrounding the video, and statements from those involved.

Background and Context

Uschi Glas, a well-known German actress, participated in a highly publicized Covid-19 vaccination campaign initiated by the German government and health authorities. The campaign aimed to encourage vaccination uptake among the public, particularly targeting older demographics who may be hesitant. As part of this effort, notable figures, including Glas, were invited to receive their vaccinations on camera to set a public example.

The video in question was widely shared on social and mainstream media, depicting Glas at a vaccination center, interacting with medical staff, and receiving an injection. Soon after its release, some social media users began to scrutinize the footage. They claimed that the vaccination was staged, pointing to aspects of the video such as the angle of the camera, the absence of visible vaccine in the syringe, or the sequence of events as evidence supporting their assertions.

Analysis of the Claim

The core claim is that Uschi Glas’s vaccination was staged, meaning she did not actually receive the vaccine during the filming of the government campaign video. To assess this, it is essential to distinguish between the staging of an event for publicity and the authenticity of the vaccination itself.

First, it is common practice for public health campaigns to film or photograph public figures receiving vaccines to encourage public participation. These events are often carefully choreographed to ensure clarity and impact in the final video, sometimes requiring multiple takes or specific camera angles. However, this does not inherently mean that the vaccinations are fake or staged in a misleading manner.

Uschi Glas has publicly affirmed that she did indeed receive the Covid-19 vaccine during the campaign event. Medical staff present at the center also confirmed that the vaccination was administered as shown in the video. There is no credible evidence to suggest that the injection was simulated, nor have health authorities or reputable media organizations identified any wrongdoing or deception in the recording or broadcast of the event.

Furthermore, the intention behind such campaign videos is to provide transparency and foster trust. Filming a staged vaccination—where no actual medicine is administered—would be counterproductive and, if discovered, would severely undermine public confidence in the campaign and its participants.

Conclusion

While the video of Uschi Glas’s Covid-19 vaccination was indeed part of a government campaign and filmed for publicity purposes, there is no substantiated evidence that the vaccination itself was staged or fake. The campaign’s objective was to encourage vaccination, and all available information supports that Glas was genuinely vaccinated during the event. Therefore, the claim that her vaccination was staged for the video is not supported by the facts.

A recent social media post claims that a video depicting a man moving inside a body bag is evidence that the Coronavirus pandemic is staged. According to the post, the apparent movement of a living person in a body bag during a news broadcast or behind-the-scenes footage invalidates the severity of COVID-19 and suggests that the pandemic is a hoax orchestrated for undisclosed purposes.

This claim has circulated widely since early 2020, often accompanying videos or images from news segments, behind-the-scenes reports, or social media uploads. The most prominent versions show individuals believed to be deceased in body bags, with one or more moving, adjusting themselves, or visibly breathing. These videos have been shared as purported proof that the pandemic is not real and that media outlets are faking deaths to create panic or enforce control.

To assess this claim, it is important to provide context about how such footage is typically produced. During the height of the pandemic, many news organizations and public awareness campaigns sought to convey the gravity of the COVID-19 crisis using visual storytelling. In some cases, they recreated hospital scenes using actors or volunteers to represent patients and victims, both for privacy concerns and to avoid graphic or distressing images of actual deceased individuals. Behind-the-scenes footage from such productions, if not clearly labeled, can easily be misconstrued as evidence of deception.

Fact-checking the specific scenario referenced in the social media post reveals that most widely circulated videos of this nature originate from behind-the-scenes footage or news bloopers. For instance, one viral video came from a Russian news segment where a person inside a body bag moved during a live report. Follow-up investigations revealed that the footage was taken while reporters were setting up a scene to illustrate the impact of COVID-19, using volunteers rather than actual bodies. The movement was due to the volunteer adjusting themselves and was not intended to mislead viewers into believing they were witnessing real deaths.

Moreover, there is no credible evidence to support the claim that the pandemic is staged based on these videos. The existence of staged or recreated footage does not invalidate the overwhelming scientific and medical consensus regarding the reality of COVID-19. Health organizations worldwide have documented millions of cases and deaths, supported by hospital data, death certificates, and excess mortality statistics.

In summary, while videos showing apparent movement in body bags may appear suspicious without context, they do not constitute evidence that the Coronavirus pandemic is staged. These videos are often misrepresented or taken out of context, stemming from media productions or reenactments intended to raise awareness or respect privacy. The core claim that such footage proves the pandemic is a hoax is unfounded and misleading. The pandemic’s reality is supported by extensive medical documentation and global scientific agreement.

As the world grappled with the COVID-19 pandemic, governments instituted lockdown measures aiming to slow the spread of the virus and protect public health systems from being overwhelmed. However, a social media post has circulated widely, claiming that these lockdowns led to an increase in heart attacks, deaths from stroke, depression, and child abuse. The post further asserts that 50,000 cancer operations were postponed as a result of these measures. This article examines the accuracy of these claims by evaluating available evidence and providing context for the complex impacts of pandemic restrictions.

Lockdowns and Medical Emergencies

One of the core assertions is that lockdowns caused a rise in heart attacks and deaths from stroke. Data from several countries suggest that, during the height of lockdowns, emergency room visits for heart attack and stroke did in fact decrease. However, this does not necessarily mean the actual incidence declined; rather, many experts believe people avoided hospitals out of fear of contracting the virus or because they did not want to burden the healthcare system. This avoidance likely led to more severe outcomes and deaths at home. While some regions observed increased out-of-hospital cardiac arrests, it is not universally true that heart attack or stroke deaths increased everywhere. The relationship appears to be complex, with some areas reporting excess deaths and others seeing little change.

Mental Health Impacts

The post also claims an increase in depression, which aligns with findings from public health studies. The pandemic and associated restrictions contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety, and symptoms of depression among both adults and children. Isolation, economic uncertainty, and disruption of daily routines were significant contributing factors. Many mental health professionals reported a surge in demand for their services during and after lockdown periods, lending credibility to the claim about rising depression rates.

Child Abuse

The assertion that child abuse increased during lockdowns is more difficult to evaluate. While some organizations and experts warned of heightened risks due to children being isolated at home—sometimes with abusive caregivers—confirmed reports and statistics present a nuanced picture. In some regions, official reports of child abuse actually dropped, likely due to the closure of schools and reduced contact with teachers and other mandatory reporters. However, experts caution that this does not necessarily indicate a real decrease in abuse, but rather a decrease in detection and reporting during lockdown periods.

Delayed Cancer Operations

Finally, the claim that 50,000 cancer operations were postponed reflects a real and significant issue. Throughout the pandemic, many health systems postponed non-urgent surgeries and treatments to free up resources for COVID-19 patients and reduce the risk of virus transmission. Estimates do suggest that tens of thousands of scheduled cancer surgeries were delayed, especially in larger countries, leading to concerns about the long-term health impacts for those patients.

In summary, while the social media post presents a somewhat simplified and alarmist version of events, many of its claims are grounded in real concerns. Lockdowns did have significant unintended health consequences, including delayed treatments, increased mental health challenges, and possible underreporting of critical health events and abuse. However, the exact magnitude and nature of these effects varied by region, health system, and population group.

The European Medicines Agency (EMA) is responsible for monitoring the safety of medicines and vaccines in the European Union. Since the rollout of Covid-19 vaccines, the agency has maintained a pharmacovigilance database where healthcare professionals and members of the public can report suspected side effects, also known as adverse events, following vaccination. A recent social media post claims that “data by the EMA shows that there are thousands of cases of secondary effects or deaths in the context of Covid-19 vaccinations.” This article examines the accuracy of this claim, provides necessary context, and analyzes what the numbers mean.

First, it is important to understand what the EMA’s data represents. The agency collects reports of suspected adverse events, which include any health problem that occurs after vaccination, whether or not the vaccine is determined to be the cause. These reports can range from minor side effects, such as headaches or mild fever, to serious medical events, including deaths. The purpose of collecting such reports is to detect potential safety signals that might require further investigation.

The EMA’s public database does indeed show that thousands of reports of suspected side effects, including some deaths, have been submitted following Covid-19 vaccinations. However, these numbers require careful interpretation. The reporting of an adverse event does not automatically mean the vaccine caused the problem. Many of the people who received the vaccine, particularly in the early stages of the rollout, were elderly or had underlying health conditions that put them at higher risk of illness or death unrelated to vaccination.

For example, if an individual suffers a heart attack or passes away days after receiving the vaccine, their case may be reported to the EMA system as a suspected adverse event. Subsequent assessments by medical experts are then conducted to determine whether there is any evidence of a causal link between the vaccine and the event. The vast majority of reported side effects are found to be unrelated to the vaccine, or consistent with side effects known to be associated with vaccination, such as sore arms or mild fever.

Moreover, the number of adverse event reports must be viewed in the context of the scale of vaccination campaigns. Hundreds of millions of Covid-19 vaccine doses have been administered across the European Union. When large populations are vaccinated, it is statistically expected that some individuals will experience health problems, including deaths, coincidentally after vaccination, even if the vaccine played no role.

The EMA and other regulatory agencies routinely review the safety data to ensure that the benefits of Covid-19 vaccines continue to outweigh any risks. To date, the EMA has concluded that the authorized Covid-19 vaccines have a favorable safety profile and that serious side effects, including deaths proven to be linked to vaccination, are extremely rare.

In summary, while it is accurate that the EMA has received thousands of reports of suspected side effects and deaths following Covid-19 vaccinations, these reports are not definitive evidence of causation. The available evidence and ongoing monitoring indicate that Covid-19 vaccines remain safe and effective for the vast majority of people.

EMA 및 기타 규제 기관은 백신의 안전성을 지속적으로 검토하여 코로나19 백신의 이점이 위험보다 우월함을 보장합니다. 현재까지 EMA는 승인된 코로나19 백신이 우수한 안전성을 가진다고 결론을 내렸으며, 백신과 관련된 증명된 사망 사례를 포함한 심각한 부작용은 매우 드뭅니다.

결론적으로, 코로나19 백신 접종 후 수천 건의 의심되는 부작용 및 사망 사례가 EMA에 보고되었다는 사실은 정확하지만, 이러한 보고 사례가 원인을 증명하는 결정적인 증거는 아닙니다. 현재의 데이터와 지속적인 모니터링에 따르면 코로나19 백신은 대부분의 사람들에게 안전하고 효과적인 것으로 나타나고 있습니다.

A recent social media post has made several claims regarding the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), mRNA vaccines, PCR testing, Covid-19 mortality data, and the accuracy of reported infection incidence rates. In this article, we analyze each statement to assess its accuracy and provide context for readers.

The post first claims that the RKI, Germany’s leading federal government agency for disease control, "allegedly doesn't know how mRNA vaccines work." The RKI has been at the forefront of Germany’s Covid-19 response, providing scientific guidance on vaccination strategies and public health measures. The Institute has published detailed explanations on the mechanism of mRNA vaccines, explaining that these vaccines use messenger RNA to instruct cells to produce a harmless spike protein, prompting an immune response. There is no evidence to suggest that the RKI lacks understanding of mRNA vaccine technology; on the contrary, their educational materials and public statements reflect current scientific consensus.

Next, the post states that PCR tests "serve to identify people and are not appropriate for diagnosis." Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests are widely regarded as the gold standard for detecting active SARS-CoV-2 infections. They work by amplifying genetic material from the virus to detectable levels. While no test is entirely error-free, PCR testing is considered highly sensitive and specific for diagnosing Covid-19, especially when compared to antigen tests. The claim that PCR tests are used to "identify people" is incorrect; they are diagnostic tools aimed at detecting viral RNA, not at verifying personal identity.

The post further alleges that "the reported death cases by the RKI don't concern people who have died from the Covid-19." This misrepresents the RKI’s reporting methodology. The Institute records deaths of individuals who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 and reports these as Covid-19-related deaths, regardless of pre-existing conditions. This approach is in line with international standards, as it is often challenging to precisely determine the sole cause of death in patients with multiple health issues. However, the RKI also provides information on comorbidities, and excess mortality statistics are used to contextualize the broader impact of the pandemic. While this method may include some deaths where Covid-19 was not the only cause, it is misleading to claim that these deaths are unrelated to Covid-19.

Lastly, the post claims that "because of the error rate of tests, the incidence of coronavirus infections practically couldn't drop to 10." The incidence rate refers to the number of new cases per 100,000 inhabitants within a specific timeframe. While all testing comes with a margin of error, widespread PCR testing under controlled laboratory conditions has a low false positive rate. As infection levels decrease, the proportion of false positives may become more relevant, but not to the extent that it would make a low incidence rate, such as 10 per 100,000, impossible. During periods of low viral circulation, Germany and other countries have reported incidence rates at or below this level.

In summary, the claims presented in the social media post are either inaccurate or lack important context. The RKI is knowledgeable about mRNA vaccines, PCR tests are appropriate for diagnosing Covid-19, the Institute’s death reporting follows international norms, and low incidence rates are achievable despite test imperfections. Readers should be cautious about such posts and seek information from official public health sources.

Инцидентни број означава број нових случајева на 100.000 становника у одређеном временском периоду. A recent social media post claims that “thousands of intensive care beds ‘disappeared’ from official statistics in order to justify lockdown or sanitary measures.” This assertion suggests that authorities deliberately altered reported intensive care unit (ICU) bed numbers to create the impression of a more strained healthcare system, thus bolstering the case for implementing pandemic restrictions. To evaluate this claim, it is important to examine how ICU bed data are reported, the context of changing bed numbers during the COVID-19 pandemic, and whether evidence supports the accusation of intentional manipulation.

**Context and Background**

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of available ICU beds became a key metric for governments and health officials in determining the severity of healthcare system stress and the necessity of public health interventions. ICU capacity was frequently cited in public communications as a justification for lockdowns, curfews, and other sanitary measures aimed at reducing virus transmission and preventing hospitals from becoming overwhelmed.

ICU bed capacity, however, is not a fixed number. Hospitals can increase or decrease beds based on staffing, equipment, and overall demand. For example, during surges in COVID-19 cases, hospitals often converted other areas into temporary ICUs or repurposed beds from other departments. Conversely, when the immediate crisis subsided, these temporary beds were returned to their original use or closed if there was insufficient staff to operate them safely.

**Analysis of the Claim**

The claim that “thousands of intensive care beds ‘disappeared’ from official statistics” touches on real changes in reported ICU capacity but misrepresents the reasons for these changes.

First, fluctuations in ICU bed numbers during the pandemic were often due to operational realities rather than deliberate data manipulation. At the height of patient surges, hospitals reported the maximum number of beds they could possibly staff and equip—sometimes counting emergency expansions. As the crisis waned and resources were reallocated, these temporary beds were removed from the tally, leading to a decrease in reported capacity. This process reflects adjustments to actual hospital capability rather than statistical sleight of hand.

Second, health authorities in many countries clarified these changes in public briefings and technical notes, explaining that reported ICU numbers included both permanent and temporary beds during peaks. There is no credible evidence that officials systematically and secretly reduced ICU bed statistics to mislead the public or artificially justify restrictions.

Third, the justification for lockdowns and sanitary measures relied on multiple metrics, not just ICU capacity. Rising infection rates, hospital admissions, and deaths were also used as key indicators in decision-making. Focusing on ICU bed numbers alone oversimplifies the complex, multifaceted approach governments used to manage the pandemic.

**Conclusion**

While it is accurate that reported ICU bed numbers changed over time, these shifts were primarily due to transparent operational factors and real-time hospital capabilities, not a covert effort to manipulate public opinion or policy. The claim that thousands of ICU beds “disappeared” from official statistics to justify pandemic measures is misleading and not supported by the available evidence. Adjustments to ICU bed counts reflected the evolving realities faced by healthcare systems during an unprecedented global health crisis.

Untuk menilai kenyataan ini, penting untuk mengkaji bagaimana data bilik rawatan intensif dilaporkan, konteks perubahan bilangan bilik rawatan intensif semasa pandemi COVID-19, dan sama ada bukti menyokong tuduhan manipulasi secara sengaja.

**Konteks dan Latar Belakang**

Semasa pandemi COVID-19, bilangan bilik rawatan intensif yang tersedia menjadi indikator utama bagi pemerintah dan pegawai kesihatan dalam menentukan keparahan tekanan sistem kesihatan serta keperluan intervensi kesihatan awam. Kapasiti bilik rawatan intensif sering dikemukakan dalam komunikasi awam sebagai justifikasi untuk mengunci kawasan, jam malam, dan langkah kesihatan lain bertujuan mengurangkan penyebaran virus dan menghalang hospital daripada terlalu sesak.

Namun, kapasiti bilik rawatan intensif bukanlah angka yang tetap. Hospital boleh meningkatkan atau mengurangkan bilik rawatan intensif berdasarkan kepadatan staf, peralatan, dan permintaan keseluruhan. Sebagai contoh, semasa peningkatan kes kes COVID-19, hospital sering mengubah ruang lain menjadi bilik rawatan intensif sementara atau mengguna semula bilik daripada jabatan lain. Sebaliknya, apabila krisis segera berlaku, bilik sementara ini kembali kepada penggunaan asal atau ditutup sekiranya tidak ada staf yang cukup untuk mengoperasikannya secara selamat.

**Analisis Kekenyataan**

Kekenyataan bahawa "ribuan bilik rawatan intensif 'hilang' daripada statistik rasmi" menyentuh perubahan sebenar dalam kapasiti bilik rawatan intensif yang dilaporkan, tetapi menyimpang dari sebab-sebab perubahan tersebut.

Pertama, perubahan bilangan bilik rawatan intensif semasa pandemi seringkali disebabkan oleh realiti operasi, bukan manipulasi data secara sengaja. Pada puncak peningkatan pesakit, hospital melaporkan bilangan maksimum bilik rawatan intensif yang boleh dioperasikan dan dilengkapi—kadang-kadang termasuk pengembangan darurat. Apabila krisis berkurang dan sumber daya diarahkan semula, bilik sementara ini dihapuskan daripada jumlah yang dilaporkan, menyebabkan penurunan kapasiti yang dilaporkan. Proses ini mencerminkan penyesuaian kepada keupayaan hospital sebenar, bukan trik statistik.

Kedua, pihak berkuasa kesihatan di banyak negara telah menjelaskan perubahan ini dalam penyataan awam dan catatan teknikal, menjelaskan bahawa bilangan bilik rawatan intensif yang dilaporkan termasuk kedua-dua bilik tetap dan sementara semasa puncak. A social media post circulating online claims that current Covid-19 vaccines facilitate "immune evasion" by the coronavirus and thereby encourage the emergence of more dangerous viral mutations. The post further asserts that, for this reason, vaccines are ineffective in fighting the pandemic. This article examines these assertions, providing context, analyzing the claim, and assessing its accuracy based on current scientific understanding.

To begin, it is important to understand what "immune evasion" means in the context of viruses and vaccines. Immune evasion refers to the ability of a virus to avoid detection or neutralization by the body's immune system, often through mutations that alter the virus's structure. The concern raised in the post centers on the idea that widespread vaccination could pressure the virus to evolve in ways that help it escape vaccine-induced immunity, potentially resulting in variants that are more transmissible or severe.

However, the scientific consensus does not support the notion that Covid-19 vaccines inherently drive the development of more dangerous variants. Vaccines work by training the immune system to recognize and respond to specific components of the virus, most notably the spike protein in the case of Covid-19. By reducing the number of infections, vaccines limit the opportunities for the virus to replicate and mutate. This, in turn, decreases the overall likelihood of new variants emerging.

It is true that viruses mutate naturally over time, and that both vaccinated and unvaccinated populations can contribute to the emergence of variants. Some mutations may help the virus partially evade immune defenses, leading to so-called "breakthrough infections" among vaccinated individuals. However, current Covid-19 vaccines remain highly effective at preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death, even against many variants. Moreover, most evidence suggests that variants of concern have emerged primarily in areas with high transmission rates and large numbers of unvaccinated people, where the virus has more opportunities to replicate and mutate.

The assertion that vaccines are "ineffective in fighting the pandemic" is contradicted by real-world data. Since the introduction of Covid-19 vaccines, countries with high vaccination rates have generally seen significant reductions in severe cases and deaths. Vaccination campaigns have been a cornerstone of public health strategies to control the pandemic, complementing other measures such as masking, testing, and social distancing.

In summary, while the evolution of the coronavirus is an ongoing process and variants capable of some immune evasion have emerged, there is no evidence that Covid-19 vaccines encourage more dangerous mutations or that they are ineffective. On the contrary, vaccines remain a critical tool in reducing transmission, preventing severe disease, and ultimately controlling the pandemic. The claim that vaccines facilitate dangerous immune evasion and are thus ineffective is not supported by current scientific understanding.

A claim circulating on social media alleges that German politician and scientist Karl Lauterbach has proposed the introduction of mandatory COVID-19 vaccination for newborns, specifically with the AstraZeneca vaccine. This assertion has generated significant concern and debate, raising questions about its accuracy and the current policies surrounding COVID-19 vaccinations in Germany.

Karl Lauterbach is a prominent figure in German politics, serving as the Federal Minister of Health since December 2021. He is also known for his background in medicine and public health, often providing expert commentary and guidance throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. Since taking office, Lauterbach has played a key role in shaping Germany’s response to the pandemic, including vaccination strategies, public health measures, and communication with the public.

To assess the validity of the claim, it is important to consider both Germany’s official vaccination recommendations and Lauterbach’s public statements. As of now, the Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) in Germany has not recommended COVID-19 vaccination for newborns or infants. The committee’s guidelines have focused on vaccinating adults, adolescents, and, in some cases, children over the age of five, particularly those at higher risk. There is no approved COVID-19 vaccine for use in newborns in Germany, nor is there a policy mandating vaccination for this age group.

Furthermore, the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine, which was among the first vaccines authorized for emergency use during the pandemic, has not been a part of Germany’s vaccination strategy for infants or young children. Due to rare but serious side effects such as blood clotting events, the use of the AstraZeneca vaccine in Germany has been restricted to certain adult age groups. Most pediatric vaccination efforts in Germany have relied on mRNA vaccines developed by companies such as Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, which have received regulatory approval for use in older children and adolescents, but not infants or newborns.

A thorough review of Karl Lauterbach’s public statements and policy proposals reveals no evidence that he has called for, proposed, or supported mandatory COVID-19 vaccination for newborns, with any vaccine, including AstraZeneca. In fact, Lauterbach’s approach has consistently emphasized voluntary vaccination, clear communication of vaccine benefits, and prioritization of higher-risk groups according to scientific guidance. There have been discussions in Germany about vaccine mandates for certain adult populations, such as healthcare workers, but not for infants or newborns.

In conclusion, the claim that Karl Lauterbach has proposed mandatory COVID-19 vaccination for newborns with the AstraZeneca vaccine is unfounded. Current German policy does not support such a measure, there is no approved vaccine for newborns, and Lauterbach has made no such proposal. The spread of this misinformation highlights the need for careful scrutiny of public health claims, particularly when they concern sensitive topics such as childhood vaccination.

On social media, a recent post claimed that due to a nighttime curfew, 650 people were blocked inside Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) until 5 a.m. from Saturday to Sunday, while hundreds of police officers waited outside the terminal and controlled people. This post has drawn significant attention, raising concerns about airport operations, passenger safety, and the role of law enforcement during overnight hours at Berlin’s main airport. This article examines the claim in detail, providing context and a thorough fact-check.

**Background: BER Airport Nighttime Operations**

Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) is subject to a strict nighttime curfew. The airport’s flight operations are generally prohibited between midnight and 5 a.m., except for emergencies or special exemptions. The curfew is designed to minimize noise for neighboring communities and is strictly enforced. While flight operations cease, the terminal itself remains open and staffed, with security and basic services available for late-arriving or early-departing passengers.

**The Incident in Question**

According to the social media post, 650 people were blocked inside the airport overnight because of the curfew, and hundreds of police officers were outside, “controlling” those inside the terminal. The post implies a situation where passengers were detained against their will, possibly under heavy police presence.

**Fact-Checking the Core Claims**

1. **Were 650 people blocked inside BER overnight?**
   It is true that, on certain occasions—often because of delayed or rescheduled flights—passengers may have to remain in the terminal during the curfew hours. On the night in question, reports indicate that approximately 650 travelers were present in the terminal, many of whom were waiting for early morning departures or had arrived late and were unable to leave the airport due to lack of public transportation or other logistical reasons. On social media, a widely shared image claims to show an aerial view of an anti-lockdown protest in London on April 24, 2021. The image purportedly depicts a large crowd gathering to demonstrate against ongoing COVID-19 restrictions in the United Kingdom. This fact-check examines the accuracy of the claim, verifies the context of the image, and provides additional background on anti-lockdown protests in London during this period.

To begin, the date mentioned—April 24, 2021—coincides with a known wave of demonstrations across the UK. At that time, the British government was gradually lifting some COVID-19 restrictions, but several measures remained in place, prompting protests from groups opposed to lockdowns and related health mandates. In London, various rallies took place throughout the spring of 2021, particularly in central locations such as Hyde Park and Oxford Street.

The image in question reportedly offers an aerial perspective, showing a dense gathering of people moving through city streets. To assess the authenticity of the claim, one must consider two factors: whether a protest occurred in London on April 24, 2021, and whether the image indeed depicts that event.

Reports confirm that on April 24, 2021, thousands of people participated in an anti-lockdown march in central London. Protesters walked from Hyde Park, along Oxford Street, and through other prominent areas, voicing opposition to ongoing coronavirus restrictions. The demonstration was well-attended and drew significant media coverage, including photographs and videos captured both at ground level and from elevated points. Police presence was visible, but the event remained largely peaceful.

Comparing the widely circulated aerial photo with verified images from news agencies and eyewitness accounts reveals notable similarities. The crowd size, route, and identifiable landmarks match those documented during the April 24 protest. The aerial vantage point is consistent with drone footage and rooftop photography seen in media coverage from that day. There is no evidence to suggest that the image has been misattributed or taken from a different protest or location.

It is also worth noting that anti-lockdown protests in London were part of a broader movement seen in other cities across Europe during the spring of 2021. Many participants raised concerns about personal freedoms, vaccine mandates, and the economic impact of prolonged restrictions. These protests were often organized via social media and attracted a diverse cross-section of the public.

In conclusion, the claim that an aerial image shows an anti-lockdown protest in London on April 24, 2021, is supported by available evidence. The photograph accurately reflects a real event and corresponds with independent reports from the day. This case highlights the importance of verifying dates, locations, and context when assessing viral content related to public demonstrations.

A recent social media post claims that a two-year-old girl in the United States was vaccinated with the Pfizer/BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine at the end of February and died six days later. This post has been widely shared, fueling concerns and questions about vaccine safety in young children. A thorough examination of the facts, background, and available data provides important context for this claim.

First, it is important to understand the timeline of COVID-19 vaccine authorization for young children in the U.S. The Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine was initially authorized for adults and older teens, with emergency use authorization for children ages 5 to 11 granted in October 2021. The vaccine was not authorized for children under five years of age until June 2022. Therefore, any claim about a two-year-old receiving the Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine prior to June 2022 would not align with the official vaccine rollout and would have been outside standard medical practice unless part of a clinical trial.

The claim states that the child died six days after vaccination. Whenever a death occurs in proximity to vaccination, it is natural for people to ask whether there is a causal link. In the U.S., adverse events following vaccination are reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), a national early warning system to detect possible safety problems with vaccines. VAERS accepts and records reports from anyone, including healthcare professionals and the public. It is important to note that a report to VAERS does not confirm that a vaccine caused an adverse event, only that an event occurred after vaccination.

There have been unverified reports circulated online, sometimes referencing VAERS, of deaths in young children following COVID-19 vaccination. However, health authorities, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), regularly review and investigate these reports. To date, there is no confirmed evidence of a causal relationship between the Pfizer/BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine and death in young children. When rare adverse events are identified, they are thoroughly investigated, and appropriate actions are taken to update guidance and inform the public.

Additionally, vaccine clinical trials for young children are designed with rigorous safety monitoring. The trials for the under-five age group included thousands of participants, and no deaths were attributed to the vaccine during the trials. While serious adverse events can occur in any large population, the overall safety profile of the Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine in children has been closely monitored and found to be favorable.

In summary, the claim that a two-year-old girl in the U.S. died six days after receiving the Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine lacks verifiable supporting evidence and does not align with the official timeline of vaccine authorization for that age group. Isolated reports of adverse events are investigated, but no causal link has been established between the vaccine and deaths in very young children. The Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine continues to be monitored for safety, and health authorities emphasize that the benefits of vaccination outweigh the known and potential risks.

Dette innlegget har blitt mye delt, og det har oppstått bekymringer og spørsmål om vaksinesikkerheten hos unge barn. En grundig gjennomgang av fakta, bakgrunn og tilgjengelige data gir viktig kontekst til dette påstanden.

Først og fremst er det viktig å forstå tiden for autorisering av COVID-19-vaksinen for unge barn i USA. Pfizer/BioNTechs vaksine ble opprinnelig autorisert for voksne og eldre ungdommer, og nødsbruk autorisering for barn mellom fem og elleve år ble gitt i oktober 2021. Vaksinen ble ikke autorisert for barn under fem år før juni 2022. Derfor vil enhver påstand om at en toårig jente ble vaksinert med Pfizer/BioNTechs vaksine før juni 2022 ikke stemme med den offisielle vaksineringstiden og ville vært utenfor standard medisinsk praksis, med unntak av en klinisk prøving.

Påstanden sier at barnet døde seks dager etter vaksinasjonen. Når en død skjer i nærheten av en vaksinasjon, er det naturlig å spørre om det er en kausal sammenheng. I USA rapporteres bivirkninger etter vaksinasjon til Vaccines Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), et nasjonalt tidligvarselsystem for å oppdage mulige sikkerhetsproblemer med vaksiner. VAERS aksepterer og registrerer rapporter fra enhver, inkludert helsepersonell og det offentlige. Det er viktig å merke seg at en rapport til VAERS ikke beviser at vaksinen forårsaket en bivirkning, bare at en hendelse skjedde etter vaksinasjonen.

Det har vært circulert uverifiserte rapporter på nett, noen ganger med referanser til VAERS, om dødsfall hos unge barn etter å ha fått en COVID-19-vaksine. Likevel gjennomgår helsemyndigheter, inkludert Sentret for sykdomsforebygging (CDC) og Food and Drug Administration (FDA), disse rapportene regelmessig og undersøker dem. Tidligere har det ikke vært bevis for en kausal sammenheng mellom Pfizer/BioNTechs COVID-19-vaksine og dødsfall hos unge barn. Når seldje bivirkninger oppdages, undersøkes de grundig, og det tas hensyn til å oppdatere retningslinjer og informere det offentlige.

Kliniske prøver for unge barn er designert med sterkt sikkerhetsovervåking. Prøvene for barn under fem år inkluderte tusenvis av deltakere, og ingen dødsfall ble tilskrevet vaksinen under prøvene. Selv om alvorlige bivirkninger kan oppstå i enhver stor befolkning, har den overordnede sikkerhetsprofilen til Pfizer/BioNTechs vaksine hos barn blitt tett overvåket og funnet tilfredsstillende.

Samlet sett mangler påstanden om at en toårig jente i USA døde seks dager etter å ha fått Pfizer/BioNTechs vaksine verifisert støtte og stemmer ikke med den offisielle tiden for autorisering av vaksinen for dette aldersgruppen. Isolerede rapporter om bivirkninger blir undersøkt, men det har ikke vært opprettet en kausal sammenheng mellom vaksinen og dødsfall hos svært unge barn. Pfizer/BioNTechs vaksine fortsetter å bli overvåket for sikkerhet, og helsemyndigheter understreker at fordeler med vaksinasjon overstiger de kjente og potensielle risikoen.

A photograph circulating on social media shows a bustling terrace at a café or restaurant, reportedly taken on April 24 in Basel, Switzerland. The image depicts numerous patrons sitting in close proximity without face masks. The accompanying post claims this scene demonstrates a stark contrast between Switzerland and neighboring Germany: despite similar COVID-19 incidence rates at the time, the Swiss public was not "subdued" by pandemic restrictions, implying a more relaxed approach compared to Germany.

To assess this claim, it is important to examine three core aspects: the authenticity of the photo and its setting, the comparative COVID-19 incidence rates in late April, and the respective public health measures in place in Switzerland and Germany at that time.

First, Basel is a prominent Swiss city near the borders with France and Germany. The setting—an outdoor café terrace—matches the description in the post. Basel’s café culture, especially in the spring, often draws crowds to outdoor spaces, making such a scene plausible. There is no evidence to suggest the image is staged or misrepresented in terms of location or date, assuming the metadata or original source corroborates the time and place.

Turning to the COVID-19 situation in late April, both Switzerland and Germany were experiencing significant numbers of new infections in the spring of 2021. Daily case rates in Switzerland were comparable to those in Germany, with both countries grappling with the ongoing third wave of the pandemic. This context supports the post’s assertion that incidence levels were similar.

However, the regulations governing public life differed markedly between the two countries. Switzerland, at that point, had begun to cautiously ease certain restrictions. Notably, on April 19, 2021, the Swiss government allowed the reopening of outdoor restaurant and café terraces, provided that health protocols such as seating limits and distancing between tables were observed. Masks were not required for diners seated at tables outdoors, but were mandated when moving around the premises or using restrooms.

In contrast, Germany maintained stricter measures in the same period. Many federal states kept restaurants and cafés closed for both indoor and outdoor dining. Mask mandates were also more broadly enforced in public spaces, and there was significant debate about further tightening measures as case numbers remained high. The stricter German approach reflected a more cautious stance, often described by critics as heavy-handed or restrictive.

The social media post’s underlying claim is that Switzerland’s relatively relaxed approach allowed for more personal freedom, as exemplified by maskless gatherings on café terraces, while Germany enforced tighter controls despite similar epidemiological circumstances. This is broadly accurate: Switzerland did permit limited outdoor dining and allowed patrons to remove masks at tables, while Germany generally did not.

In summary, the photograph aligns with the Swiss policies in place in late April 2021, and the comparison to Germany’s stricter approach is factually supported. While both countries had similar rates of COVID-19 infections, their responses diverged, leading to visible differences in daily life—such as the scene depicted on Basel’s café terraces. The post’s core claim reflects the reality of differing national strategies during this phase of the pandemic.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated claiming that Annalena Baerbock, the chancellor candidate of Germany’s Green Party, was photographed having physical contact with other people. The implication behind this claim, especially in the context of ongoing public health concerns, is that Baerbock may have disregarded social distancing guidelines.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the available evidence, provide necessary background about the political and public health context, and consider the intent and implications of such a post.

**Background and Context**

Annalena Baerbock has been a prominent figure in German politics, particularly since her nomination as the Green Party’s candidate for chancellor in the 2021 federal elections. As with many politicians, Baerbock’s public appearances and actions are closely scrutinized, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, when adherence to health protocols has become a subject of public interest and debate.

Since the onset of the pandemic, German authorities have issued varying guidelines regarding physical contact, mask usage, and social distancing, depending on infection rates and local regulations. Politicians have often been expected to set an example for the public by adhering to these protocols during campaign events and public appearances.

**Analysis of the Claim**

The social media post in question asserts that recent pictures show Baerbock having physical contact with others. Fact-checking this claim involves two key elements: verifying the existence of such photographs and analyzing the context in which physical contact occurred.

Upon review, there are indeed photographs from campaign events and public appearances where Annalena Baerbock is seen engaging in physical gestures with others, such as handshakes, hugs, or placing a hand on someone’s shoulder. Such gestures are common in political contexts, often as a sign of camaraderie or support. However, the timing and context of these photographs are crucial.

Some images date from periods when Germany had relaxed certain social distancing measures or when outdoor events allowed for limited contact, especially among individuals who were vaccinated, tested, or recovered from COVID-19. In other cases, physical contact appears brief and occurs while other precautions, such as mask-wearing, are observed.

It is also important to note that over the course of the pandemic, politicians across the spectrum have occasionally been seen in moments of physical contact, sometimes apologizing if these moments were perceived as breaches of protocol.

**Conclusion**

The core claim of the social media post—that recent pictures show Annalena Baerbock having physical contact with other people—is accurate in a literal sense. Such images exist and are publicly available. However, the context is essential: the contact generally occurred within the bounds of evolving public health guidelines, and there is no evidence to suggest that Baerbock intentionally disregarded public health rules or engaged in reckless behavior. The social media post, while factually correct, omits this critical context and may be interpreted in a misleading manner if not understood within the full scope of the situation.

A video circulating on social media features a person identified as a US virologist who announces intentions to sue the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and asserts that the coronavirus does not exist. This claim has garnered attention online, prompting concerns about public health misinformation and confusion regarding the existence of SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic. This article examines the background of these claims and provides a detailed analysis of their validity.

To begin, the CDC—short for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention—is the leading national public health institute in the United States. The CDC has played a central role in tracking, studying, and providing guidance on COVID-19 since its emergence in late 2019. The claim that a US virologist intends to sue the CDC is not unprecedented; various individuals and organizations have publicly criticized the agency over its pandemic response. However, such lawsuits rarely center on the existence of the virus itself and are more commonly related to policy decisions, mandates, or alleged mishandling of information.

The more striking assertion made in the video is that "the coronavirus does not exist." This statement directly contradicts the extensive scientific evidence amassed since the onset of the pandemic. SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, was first identified in Wuhan, China, and its genetic sequence was rapidly published and shared worldwide. Laboratories across the globe have isolated and studied the virus, confirming its structure, method of infection, and impact on human health. The coronavirus belongs to a well-known family of viruses, including previous strains such as SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV, both responsible for earlier outbreaks.

The existence of SARS-CoV-2 is corroborated by thousands of peer-reviewed studies, epidemiological data, and clinical laboratory analyses. The virus has been visualized using electron microscopy and sequenced using advanced genetic techniques. Diagnostic tests—including PCR and antigen assays—specifically detect components of the virus, which have been consistently found in infected individuals. Furthermore, vaccines developed to combat COVID-19 target the virus’s spike protein, demonstrating both the specificity and real-world impact of scientific understanding about its existence.

The claim that coronavirus does not exist is a recurring theme among certain groups who question established science or promote conspiracy theories. Such statements are not supported by any credible scientific institution or expert consensus. The consequences of spreading misinformation about the existence of the virus are significant, as they can undermine public health efforts, reduce compliance with mitigation measures, and potentially endanger lives.

As for the legal threat against the CDC mentioned in the video, while individuals are free to pursue litigation, courts rely on factual evidence and established science. Lawsuits based on the assertion that the coronavirus does not exist are unlikely to succeed, as the existence of the virus is a settled matter in the scientific and medical communities.

In summary, the social media video’s core claim that “the coronavirus does not exist” is unequivocally false. SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for the global COVID-19 pandemic, has been extensively documented, studied, and combated through international scientific collaboration. While criticism of public health authorities is not uncommon, it is essential to distinguish between policy debates and factual inaccuracies. Misinformation about the existence of the virus poses a serious risk to public health and should be countered with clear, evidence-based communication.

A social media post recently claimed that vaccinations lead to a cytokine storm and organ failure. This assertion has generated concern among some readers, raising questions about vaccine safety and the biological mechanisms involved in immune responses. In this article, we examine the claim, provide scientific context, and analyze whether vaccinations are linked to cytokine storm and organ failure.

To understand the core claim, it’s important to clarify the terms involved. A cytokine storm is an excessive immune response where the body releases large amounts of cytokines—proteins that help signal and regulate the immune system. While cytokines are essential for fighting infections, an uncontrolled release can cause severe inflammation, tissue damage, and, in extreme cases, organ failure. Cytokine storms are most commonly associated with severe infections, such as influenza, COVID-19, and certain autoimmune conditions.

Vaccines are designed to train the immune system to recognize and fight disease-causing organisms, such as viruses and bacteria, without causing illness. Most vaccines contain weakened or inactivated parts of a pathogen, or its genetic material, prompting the body to produce a controlled immune response. This process typically results in mild, temporary side effects, such as soreness at the injection site, mild fever, or fatigue.

The claim that vaccinations cause cytokine storms and organ failure suggests that the immune response produced by vaccines is excessive and dangerous. However, this scenario is not supported by current scientific understanding or clinical evidence. Vaccines are rigorously tested for safety and efficacy before approval. They are specifically formulated to elicit a measured immune response, strong enough to generate protection but not to provoke excessive inflammation.

Reports of cytokine storms are extremely rare following vaccination. When they do occur, they are typically linked to underlying health conditions or immune system disorders, not to the vaccine itself. The vast majority of individuals who receive vaccines do not experience severe adverse reactions. Serious complications, such as organ failure, are exceedingly uncommon and are usually related to severe allergic reactions or pre-existing illnesses, not to the immune response intended by the vaccine.

It is important to recognize that the risk of cytokine storm and organ failure is far higher with many infectious diseases that vaccines are designed to prevent. For instance, severe cases of influenza or COVID-19 can trigger cytokine storms and subsequent organ damage. Vaccination reduces the risk of these complications by preventing infection or lessening disease severity.

In summary, the claim that vaccinations lead to cytokine storm and organ failure does not reflect the overwhelming evidence from clinical trials and monitoring systems. Vaccines are a safe and effective tool for preventing infectious diseases and the severe complications associated with them. While adverse reactions can occur, they are rare and typically much less severe than the complications caused by the diseases themselves. Public health experts maintain that vaccination is crucial for individual and community health, and misinformation about vaccine safety can undermine these efforts.

article_content:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments around the world implemented a variety of restrictions and public health measures to control the spread of the virus. These included lockdowns, social distancing rules, mask mandates, and limitations on gatherings. In Germany, as in many other countries, enforcement of these measures became a topic of public debate and, at times, controversy. A recent social media post claims that "The German government called for citizens to report neighbours who breach measures against COVID-19." This article examines the veracity of this claim by analyzing the context, the government's actions, and the public response during the pandemic.

To begin with, the federal structure of Germany means that while the national government provides recommendations and legislative frameworks, the enforcement and implementation of COVID-19 measures were largely handled at the state (Länder) and municipal levels. Throughout the pandemic, various German states and cities introduced hotlines and online portals where individuals could report breaches of COVID-19 regulations, such as illegal parties, failure to wear masks, or violations of quarantine orders.

It is accurate to state that some authorities encouraged citizens to notify them if they observed violations. The intention behind these measures was to ensure compliance and protect public health, given the difficulty of policing millions of people in private and public spaces. Local authorities argued that community vigilance was necessary to identify and address non-compliance that could contribute to new outbreaks.

However, the claim that "the German government called for citizens to report neighbours" requires careful clarification. The federal government in Berlin did not issue a direct, nationwide call for citizens to report on their neighbours. Instead, the encouragement to report breaches typically came from local or state officials, and was often framed as a means to support enforcement rather than to create a culture of surveillance or mistrust.

Moreover, the idea of "reporting neighbours" specifically evokes concerns about privacy and historical sensitivities in Germany, where surveillance and informing on others have negative connotations due to the country's experiences in the 20th century. Public discussion around these reporting mechanisms was often contentious, with critics warning that such encouragement could erode social trust. In response, some officials clarified that reports should be made only in cases of serious or repeated violations, and stressed the importance of responsible use of reporting channels.

In summary, while it is true that some German authorities set up mechanisms for citizens to report breaches of COVID-19 measures, the claim that "the German government called for citizens to report neighbours" somewhat oversimplifies the situation. The calls to report were not uniform, not always directed at "neighbours" specifically, and were not initiated at the federal level. The measures were part of broader efforts to enforce pandemic regulations, and they sparked significant debate within German society about the balance between public health and personal privacy.

Selama pandemi COVID-19, pemerintah di berbagai negara di dunia menerapkan berbagai pembatasan dan kebijakan kesehatan masyarakat untuk mengendalikan penyebaran virus. Ini mencakup lockdown, aturan jarak sosial, peraturan wajib memakai masker, dan pembatasan pertemuan. Di Jerman, seperti di banyak negara lainnya, penerapan kebijakan ini menjadi topik perdebatan publik dan bahkan kontroversi. Sebuah postingan media sosial baru-baru ini menyatakan bahwa "Pemerintah Jerman meminta warga melaporkan tetangganya yang melanggar aturan pencegahan COVID-19." Artikel ini mengeksplorasi kebenaran klaim tersebut dengan menganalisis konteks, tindakan pemerintah, dan respons masyarakat selama pandemi.

Sebagai permulaan, struktur federal Jerman berarti bahwa meskipun pemerintah nasional memberikan rekomendasi dan kerangka hukum, penerapan dan pelaksanaan kebijakan COVID-19 secara umum diatur oleh tingkat negara (Länder) dan kota. Selama pandemi, berbagai negara bagian dan kota di Jerman memperkenalkan hotline dan portal online di mana individu dapat melaporkan pelanggaran aturan kebijakan COVID-19, seperti pesta ilegal, tidak memakai masker, atau pelanggaran perintah karantina.

Benar untuk menyatakan bahwa beberapa otoritas mendorong warga untuk memberi tahu mereka jika mereka melihat pelanggaran. Tujuan dari kebijakan ini adalah memastikan kepatuhan dan melindungi kesehatan publik, mengingat kesulitan memantau jutaan orang di ruang publik dan pribadi. Otoritas lokal berargumen bahwa kewaspadaan komunitas diperlukan untuk mengidentifikasi dan menangani ketidaktahuan yang dapat berkontribusi pada wabah baru.

Namun, klaim bahwa "pemerintah Jerman meminta warga melaporkan tetangganya" memerlukan penjelasan yang hati-hati. Pemerintah federal di Berlin tidak mengeluarkan pernyataan langsung dan nasional yang meminta warga melaporkan tetangganya. Sebaliknya, dorongan untuk melaporkan pelanggaran biasanya datang dari pejabat daerah atau negara bagian, dan sering kali disampaikan sebagai cara untuk mendukung pelaksanaan kebijakan, bukan untuk menciptakan budaya pengawasan atau ketidakpercayaan.

Selain itu, gagasan "melaporkan tetangga" secara spesifik memicu kekhawatiran tentang privasi dan sensitivitas sejarah di Jerman, di mana pengawasan dan melaporkan orang lain memiliki konotasi negatif karena pengalaman negara tersebut di abad ke-20. Diskusi publik mengenai mekanisme pelaporan sering kali kontroversial, dengan kritikus memperingatkan bahwa dorongan semacam ini dapat mengikis kepercayaan sosial. Sebagai tanggapan, beberapa pejabat memperjelas bahwa pelaporan hanya seharusnya dilakukan dalam kasus pelanggaran serius atau berulang, serta menekankan pentingnya penggunaan saluran pelaporan secara bertanggung jawab.

Secara keseluruhan, meskipun benar bahwa beberapa otoritas Jerman memperkenalkan mekanisme bagi warga untuk melaporkan pelanggaran aturan kebijakan COVID-19, klaim bahwa "pemerintah Jerman meminta warga melaporkan tetangganya" agak menyederhanakan situasi. Dorongan untuk melaporkan tidak seragam, tidak selalu ditujukan secara khusus kepada "tetangga", dan tidak dimulai di tingkat federal. Kebijakan tersebut merupakan bagian dari upaya yang lebih luas untuk menerapkan regulasi pandemi, dan memicu perdebatan signifikan dalam masyarakat Jerman mengenai keseimbangan antara kesehatan publik dan privasi pribadi.
